relations.label: If the operator crosses the fixed point without the replacement in hand, every lead time that could have run inside the runway is spent, and what remains are the lead times that could not begin until the death; the floor passes from a height above zero to a gap after it, and the operator has left this map for survival-floors, whose floors are what the gap is bridged with.

relations.from: Place in line: the replacement arrives when others leave or when an event no one schedules occurs, as the transplant list, the social-housing list, the visa quota, the berth, so the lead time is a position moved by others' exits or by a priority score and the wait has a distribution and no date; the carrier is the queue's rule of order, it is shortened by a side channel, the living donor, the private lane, or by a rush fee where one is sold, whose existence tells the operator that the wait was a queue and prices the floor, and it is faked by 'on the list' read as a date; not Once a year, where the date is known and the wait is to it, since here the date is unknown and the only knowable thing is the place.
relations.to: Gestation: the replacement must grow, as the crop that takes a season, the herd that takes a gestation and a weaning, timber, a barrel's years, an orchard's years before it bears, so the lead time is a count of elapsed time no money converts; the carrier is the thing's own rate of becoming, it is shortened only by buying the thing at a later stage, a heifer rather than a calf, a running business rather than a plan, which is buying someone else's elapsed time, and it is faked by the seed in the ground counted as the crop; not Staggered stand, which is the purchase of starting, since Gestation is the reason the stand is the only purchase, and not Calendar with nothing in it, since here the time is an ingredient and something is growing in it.
relations.label: If someone sells a shorter wait at any price, a rush lane, a private list, a side channel, then the wait was a place and the fee prices the floor; if no one sells one, the wait may still be a queue where expediting is forbidden, a rule's sentence, or a window, and only if something is growing in it was it an ingredient, so the expedite market is the operator's first probe and its absence sends them to the second, whether anything grows, anyone watches, or a rule names the date; the fork is real, but only one of its arms is decided by the fee.

relations.from: Understudy: the replacement is finished before it is needed and waits, as the standby generator, the theatre's understudy, the second goalkeeper, the named successor, the spare transformer in the yard, so the lead time is zero and the floor drops to the wind-down bill alone; the lead time was run to completion in advance, the carrier is an idle copy and its upkeep, it is shortened to nothing at the price of carrying a thing that earns nothing, and it is faked by the spare never exercised, the generator that will not start, the backup never once restored, the understudy who never rehearsed, so the drill and not the spare is the purchase, since a spare's lead time is unknown until it is called; not survival-floors' Kept on call, which is the seller's retainer, since here the operator owns the copy and no other hand can call it.
relations.to: Staggered stand: where the lead time is elapsed time itself, the only purchase is a stand of replacements started at every age, as the forester who plants a cohort every year so a cutting is always ripe, the vintner's barrels of every vintage, the rancher's heifers behind the cows, the firm that is always ramping one hire and the bench of juniors behind a senior; the carrier is the carrying cost of every cohort at once, it is shortened by nothing further, since starting is the whole purchase, and it is faked by the stand with a missing cohort, the hiring freeze that leaves no one to promote ten years later, the forest with no thirty-year-olds, which is invisible until the year the absent cohort would have matured; not Understudy, which is one finished copy, since a stand is bought by starting and not by finishing, and only a stand can replace a replacement.
relations.label: If the finished spare decays while it waits, the tyre's rubber, the backup's format, the understudy's memory of the part, the successor who leaves for a live post, then the spare is itself on a lead time and must be replaced on one, so a standing spare depends on a stand of spares at every age; the lead time bought entirely ahead rests on one that can only be pre-started.

relations.from: Partner meeting: the replacement arrives on the counterparty's decision calendar rather than the operator's, as the fund's Monday partner meeting, the hiring committee that sits monthly, the credit committee that meets quarterly, the admissions round, the diocese's placement, so the lead time is the cadence of their meetings times the number of gates the decision must pass; the carrier is the counterparty's own process, it is shortened by a pre-signed paper, a standing term sheet, a pre-approved line, an offer held open, whose own fake is that the writer re-decides at exercise, as the credit line reviewed when drawn, and it is faked by the verbal yes, which is a decision not yet on their calendar; adds to runway-illusions' Watched burn, which reprices the terms, the arrival, since a counterparty can be willing and slow.
relations.to: No-shop: the counterparty's paper forbids running the search in parallel, as the term sheet's exclusivity period, the lock-out agreement, the exclusive listing, the visa system that cancels an application when a second is filed, so the lead time becomes serial and each failed candidate costs its whole exclusivity rather than its share of a spread; the carrier is the clause, it is shortened by a short exclusivity or a break fee, and it is faked by the non-binding term sheet whose one binding clause is the no-shop; the exploding offer is the same serialization from the other end, forbidding the wait rather than the search; adds to runway-illusions' Runway in shots, which counts trials, the rule that decides whether trials may run at once.
relations.label: If the counterparty's cadence is slow and it knows the operator is running the search in parallel, it protects its cadence by buying exclusivity, so the pre-signed paper that shortens the wait arrives carrying the clause that serializes it; the cure recruits the disease, and the term sheet is faster than the committee only for the one candidate it locks.

exploration.first_question: Which mechanisms set the time between a source's failing and its replacement's arrival, so that a runway must contain that time and the death line sits above zero: who holds the lead time, what shortens it, and what fakes it?
exploration.changed_question: When can the replacement's clock run relative to the source's, and what does running it do to the source? The first breath sorted lead times by who held them (a counterparty, a queue, a rule, a growing thing) and assumed each ran independently of the runway it had to fit inside. Sharpening Partner meeting against runway-illusions' waiting investor produced a lead time that lengthens as the runway shortens, so the floor is a fixed point and not a number; sharpening Understudy's fake, the spare never exercised, against Gestation showed that a finished spare is itself on a lead time and that a real-time lead time can be pre-started but never bought. The second breath then found the lead times that must run inside the dying runway and act on it (No-shop, Seeking is telling, Rising floor), the one purchase available for elapsed time (Staggered stand), the rule's empty wait (Calendar with nothing in it), and the lead times that cannot begin until the death (Starts at the funeral). The territory pointer stands and the slug is kept; the of-sentence now asks, for each item, when its clock can run.
exploration.new_member: Staggered stand: where the lead time is elapsed time itself, the only purchase is a stand of replacements started at every age, as the forester who plants a cohort every year so a cutting is always ripe, the vintner's barrels of every vintage, the rancher's heifers behind the cows, the firm that is always ramping one hire and the bench of juniors behind a senior; the carrier is the carrying cost of every cohort at once, it is shortened by nothing further, since starting is the whole purchase, and it is faked by the stand with a missing cohort, the hiring freeze that leaves no one to promote ten years later, the forest with no thirty-year-olds, which is invisible until the year the absent cohort would have matured; not Understudy, which is one finished copy, since a stand is bought by starting and not by finishing, and only a stand can replace a replacement.

priorities.item: Rising floor: the lead time lengthens as the runway shortens, as the unemployed are hired slower than the employed, the firm at three months raises slower than at twelve, the seller with a closing date gets fewer offers, so the floor is not the lead time measured from strength but the fixed point where remaining runway equals the lead time at that remaining runway, and it sits higher; the carrier is the counterparty's reading of the remaining clock as a signal about the operator rather than as a bargaining position, so the field thins, fewer counterparties engage at all and those who do add diligence, and the expected wait lengthens without any price moving; it is shortened by starting from strength, before the clock is legible, and it is faked by the lead time quoted by someone who ran it from strength, since 'it took me six weeks' was measured at another point on the curve; the thinning is observed in labour markets, the fixed point is analytical, and the extension to firms and sellers is by analogy; not Watched burn, which holds the buyer who reads the clock and waits for the price, since here the clock read as a signal removes counterparties rather than moving their terms, and the floor is a fixed point rather than a number.
priorities.why: It is the map's central claim about where operators actually die, it can be run on dated records without anyone's cooperation, and it is the probe the runway-illusions critic asked for; if lead time does not lengthen with shortening runway, the floor is a number after all and the loop with Seeking is telling is decoration.
priorities.next_question: Take ten raises or ten job searches with dates: the remaining runway (months of cash, or months of savings) on the day the search began and the days from that day to the wire or the start date; plot lead time against runway at start and draw the diagonal where the two are equal; the crossing is the fixed point, the count of searches begun below it is how many were already dead at first pitch, and the slope above it is the size of the rise.

priorities.item: Staggered stand: where the lead time is elapsed time itself, the only purchase is a stand of replacements started at every age, as the forester who plants a cohort every year so a cutting is always ripe, the vintner's barrels of every vintage, the rancher's heifers behind the cows, the firm that is always ramping one hire and the bench of juniors behind a senior; the carrier is the carrying cost of every cohort at once, it is shortened by nothing further, since starting is the whole purchase, and it is faked by the stand with a missing cohort, the hiring freeze that leaves no one to promote ten years later, the forest with no thirty-year-olds, which is invisible until the year the absent cohort would have matured; not Understudy, which is one finished copy, since a stand is bought by starting and not by finishing, and only a stand can replace a replacement.
priorities.why: Low plausibility that starting is the only purchase wherever time is the ingredient, since later-stage markets exist for cattle and companies; high generative promise, because it says a whole class of floors can be seen years ahead as a gap in an age structure, which no cash figure and no lead-time quote shows, and because it makes the missing cohort a clock that reads the year of a future death.
priorities.next_question: Take one organization's headcount by year of joining, or one forest's age classes, and find the empty cohort; predict the year in which that cohort would have been the one promoted or cut, and check whether that year shows an outside hire at that level, a promotion of someone too green, or a gap in the cut; then run the same on a fictional stand where one cohort is skipped, to see whether the gap is ever recoverable by buying a later stage or only by waiting the cohort's full age.

gate.standard: declared type, close-neighbor discriminator, boundary case, and form inference
gate.independent_review: Fable critic: admitted after repairing four items (a misfiled example moved from Gestation to Clean months, a fake overclaimed as fraud, a discriminator that was a ratio rather than a mechanism, and a central item whose carrier duplicated Watched burn), three edge labels whose antecedents could not fail as written, and a boundary claim that contradicted Release at both ends.

neighbors.left: Seeking is telling: the search for a replacement is visible to the source and shortens it, as the employer who learns of the interviews, the investor who hears the founder pitched the fund next door, the landlord who sees the boxes, the client who learns the firm is prospecting, so a lead time that must be run inside the runway shortens the runway it runs in; the carrier is the source's sight of the search, it is shortened by a discreet channel, the headhunter, the banker's confidential process, the exploratory conversation, and it is faked by the confidential process in a town of one industry; not Watched burn, where the source sees the burn, since here the source sees the cure.
neighbors.right: Rising floor: the lead time lengthens as the runway shortens, as the unemployed are hired slower than the employed, the firm at three months raises slower than at twelve, the seller with a closing date gets fewer offers, so the floor is not the lead time measured from strength but the fixed point where remaining runway equals the lead time at that remaining runway, and it sits higher; the carrier is the counterparty's reading of the remaining clock as a signal about the operator rather than as a bargaining position, so the field thins, fewer counterparties engage at all and those who do add diligence, and the expected wait lengthens without any price moving; it is shortened by starting from strength, before the clock is legible, and it is faked by the lead time quoted by someone who ran it from strength, since 'it took me six weeks' was measured at another point on the curve; the thinning is observed in labour markets, the fixed point is analytical, and the extension to firms and sellers is by analogy; not Watched burn, which holds the buyer who reads the clock and waits for the price, since here the clock read as a signal removes counterparties rather than moving their terms, and the floor is a fixed point rather than a number.
neighbors.separating_case: A founder who runs the raise through a banker's confidential process at three months of runway: no employee, customer, or landlord learns of the search, so Seeking is telling is defeated, yet every fund that opens the data room reads three months off the bank statement as a signal, fewer proceed and those that do add diligence, so Rising floor bites unaltered. In reverse, an employee with a year of savings whose manager hears of an interview: no counterparty reads a short clock yet, so no floor rises, but the source shortens. Each occurs without the other; the loop is when both do, and the fixed point belongs to Rising floor alone.

checks.boundary_case: The remaining term on the operator's own lease, or the severance owed, is a tempting nonmember and is out: it is time the operator must pay for while stopping, not time the operator must wait for an arrival, and runway-illusions' Burn you cannot put down already holds it. The net-sixty invoice is out for the same reason on the other side, since it delays reaching money already owned rather than the arrival of a replacement. A member is a wait for something to arrive that is not yet the operator's.
checks.form_inference: The map shows a loop the sequence conceals: Seeking is telling and Rising floor sit as neighbours on the itinerary, but the two edges between them say that a visible search shortens the source and a shorter source slows the search, and that the rise forces an early start exactly when seeking tells most, where searching is not customary; the fixed point belongs to Rising floor alone, and the cycle decides how early the operator meets it, not where it is. It shows an incompatibility at Ramp inside the floor → Seeking is telling: where the overlap needs the old source's hand, the old source must host its successor, so past that point one cannot both overlap and keep the search discreet; where overlap needs only that the source keep working, the antecedent fails and the incompatibility does not fire. It shows a passage between levels at Rising floor → Starts at the funeral, where the floor moves from a height above zero to a gap after it and the operator leaves this map for survival-floors. It shows a fork with a test at Place in line → Gestation, whose presence arm is decided by whether anyone sells a shorter wait and whose absence arm sends the operator to a second probe. It shows a dependency at Understudy → Staggered stand, where the lead time bought entirely ahead rests on one that can only be pre-started. And it shows a recruitment at Partner meeting → No-shop, where the paper that shortens the committee's wait carries the clause that serializes the search.
checks.target_preserved: Judged by the Fable critic in a fresh context, not a self-read: the strange members survive as mechanisms after repair, the drill rather than the spare, the stand of every age, the wait that is a sentence, the serialization sold as a cure, the lead time that cannot begin until the death, and the fixed-point floor, which the critic called the map's best idea and kept while replacing the carrier it shared with Watched burn; the critic tried to break the fork, the dependency, the recruitment, and the passage and could not.

name: investor-tells
of: A mechanism by which a founder reads an investor's real position, where the decision sits, what stage the process is in, what the fund can do, and whose politics govern it, off something the investor spends, forgoes, sequences, or signs rather than says, named with the carrier read, the state it reveals, and the case where it lies, and sorted by where the founder must stand to see it: in the public record before contact, in the room, in the following week, in the diligence, on the paper, in a move the founder must make, or only after the wire.
items: Ledger's clock: whether a yes is even available is read from the fund's own deployment record before the partner's appetite matters, since a fund in year four of a five-year investment period with half its capital uncalled must deploy and a fund that made nine investments in its first year and one in its third is holding reserves for its own portfolio, and both are visible in announced checks and filing dates before the first email; the carrier is the fund's ledger and not the partner, and it lies when the visible fund is not the vehicle that would write this check, an unannounced successor fund or an opportunity vehicle running on a different clock.

Partner's name on the door: whether the person across the table can carry a deal is read from whose name sits on the fund's last deals, its board seats and its announcements, not from the title on the website, since a venture partner, a principal, or an operating partner can refer but cannot spend; it lies most instructively at the newly made partner whose name is on nothing because their first deal is still to come, and who therefore has the strongest motive in the building to close one, and it also lies at the partner hired laterally, whose deals sit on another fund's ledger, and at funds that seat a different partner on the board than the one who sponsored the deal, where the seat list reads bandwidth and not standing.

Neighbor in the portfolio: if the fund already holds a company in the founder's market, the meeting's purpose is set before it starts, and the tell is whether the partner names the neighbor unprompted, since an undisclosed neighbor makes the meeting intelligence gathered for it; it adds to cooperative-masks' alliance proposed to inventory your capabilities the check that can be run from the portfolio page before the alliance is proposed, and it lies at a fund that runs an index strategy and will honestly own two rivals, which its ledger shows as other such pairs.

Second body: partner attention is the fund's scarcest unit, so a second partner at the second meeting means the first has spent standing inside the partnership to bring one, as a medieval charter's witness list tells a historian which magnates the king needed present, while an associate-only follow-up, however warm, is still screening; a partner who writes the follow-up in their own words at midnight but cannot bring a second body is appetite without a vote, and the tell lies at a fund of two partners, where every meeting is a partner meeting and the reading must fall back to whether the meeting was moved to the founder's site.

Who sums up: the partnership's internal rank is read in the room from who interrupts whom and who restates the deal at the end, since the one who summarizes holds the pen the others will read from on Monday, the way a newcomer in a prison yard reads rank not from size but from who is deferred to; not who came, which is Second body, but the order of speech among those who did, and it lies at partnerships that perform equality, where the reading falls back to whom the others ask the last question.

Queue interval: an interval the founder is made to wait measures this deal's rank in a queue the founder cannot see, so the days before the second meeting read the partner's queue against whatever else that partner saw this week, and after signing the days before counsel returns a standard document read the fund's closing queue and whether it is waiting on something unsaid, a co-investor, a consent, a successor fund; it adds to lead-time-floors' Partner meeting, which reads what the calendar does to the founder's runway, by reading what the interval says about the investor's ordering, and it lies whenever the interval is the fund's clock rather than the partner's, in August, in December, or under must-deploy, which is why a fast second meeting from a fund late in its period reads the ledger and not the partner.

Tense switch: an investor still deciding asks about the past, why the cohort churned, why this architecture, while an investor who has decided asks about the deal, round size, who else is in, whether there is room to lead, and the switch usually precedes any spoken yes by days; the sharpest form is the allocation question, how much can we take, which is addressed to the other investors through the founder, as an auction bidder who asks about the reserve has stopped inspecting the lot; it lies when a partner asks round size first to check the fund's check-size fit, which is a size question and not an allocation question.

Borrowed eyes: an investor who asks who else is in before any question about the company, and whose questions about the company arrive only after the answer names a lead, or never, holds a position that is a function of another investor's, so the founder is reading the wrong node and every later tell from this investor should be re-read as a tell about the lead it follows, a day late; not the same question asked first by an investor who then inspects, which checks whether the round is already spoken for, and it lies when the question is about round mechanics from a fund that never leads and honestly needs a lead to set terms, which its ledger shows as a record of follows.

Holdable sentence: an investor's words are read by whether they could later be quoted back against the speaker, so we would love to see more traction is a pass that keeps a free option on the company, while at this revenue with this retention, call me and we move in a week binds a metric, a threshold, and a date, as an employer who names a wage reopener date has conceded something and one who says we will look at it next year has not; the carrier is the cost of being quoted, and it lies when a fund rule such as a stage floor makes the vagueness honest rather than option-keeping, which is checked against the ledger.

Named objection: a no that states the objection that won, in terms particular to this company, reads as a vote that happened and a sponsor who argued and lost, since only someone who fought the objection can name it exactly, while a no attributed to the partnership in generic terms reads as a deal that never reached the room; not a specific no that is a fund rule, a stage floor or a sector the fund does not do, which is exact without any vote, and it adds to deal-deaths' Champion's single-tender want, which reads how a sponsor's leaving kills a deal, by reading from the wording of the no whether a sponsor existed at all; it lies when a partner who killed the deal alone reads back the founder's own weakest slide as the objection.

Order of asks: a request for the data room before a partner-meeting date has been set reverses the usual order, in which a partner buys in, the partnership authorizes the work, and the room is opened, so it reads a partner who lacks standing and needs the data to win the room, or a fund whose associates screen on numbers before any partner looks; it is preparation rather than screening only when the ask arrives with a date attached, and it lies at growth funds where quantitative screening precedes every partner by design.

Shopping list: diligence questions divide by whether the answer is useful to someone other than the decider, so named customers with prices, a pipeline by account, and a roadmap by quarter are transferable to a portfolio company while the reason a cohort churned is not, and the test is whether the investor accepts anonymized accounts and founder-chosen reference names, since a decider needs the shape and a shopper needs the names; it lies at late-stage funds whose cohort work needs account-level data, separated by their willingness to route it through a third-party quality-of-earnings firm that returns only the shape.

Back-channel spent: a call to a reference the founder offered is process, but a call to someone the founder did not offer, a former employee, a former investor, a rival's founder, costs the caller a favor and is spent only near the decision, so learning of it, usually from the person called, reads that the partner meeting is close and names the objection being tested; the reverse of lead-time-floors' Seeking is telling, since here the investor's search is visible to the founder, and the sharper reading is the call not made, because a term sheet issued with no back-channel is a reservation and not a decision wherever there was someone to call; it lies at large multi-stage funds whose research staff call everyone at screen, where the favor costs the partner nothing, and it is undefined at pre-seed, where no former employee, investor, or rival exists to be called and the absent call reads nothing.

Fuse length: the expiry on a term sheet is priced against when the investor expects a rival sheet to arrive, so a short fuse reveals the investor's own estimate that the founder's alternatives are good, an outside estimate of the founder's price carried by the party who will pay it, as a kidnapper's deadline reveals what the kidnapper believes the family can raise by then; it also reads the fund's clock when the close-by date is the fund's own, and it lies at funds that put a fuse on every sheet as house style, which founders who took their paper can tell you and which only Let it lapse can test.

Exclusivity as confession: the length of the no-shop the investor asks for measures the work the investor has not yet done and the room to walk it wants to keep, so sixty days from a fund that has spent no back-channel is an option and ten days from one that has is a close; it adds to lead-time-floors' No-shop, which reads what the lock does to the founder's clock, by reading what the lock's length says about the investor's remaining doubt, and it lies where the length was set by counsel's template rather than by the partner.

Term as forecast: each protective term is a bet on a future state, so the redline shows the investor's private forecast, a participating preference pricing a middling exit as likely, a full ratchet pricing a down round, super pro-rata pricing a wish for more, information rights without a seat pricing a passive hold, as an arms treaty's inspection clauses name the breach each side expects; only deviations from the fund's standard paper read, since house paper forecasts nothing, and the founder learns the standard from other founders who took it; it lies where the partner has not read what counsel sent, and where a term was carried forward from the company's own prior paper, which forecasts the last investor's fear and not this one's.

Let it lapse: some tells exist only if the founder moves, so an expiry allowed to pass by a day reads whether the fuse was real, since a re-issued sheet shows the investor feared losing the deal more than being seen to bluff and a withdrawn one shows the clock was the fund's, as a deadline a kidnapper lets pass unacted reveals the deadline was a bluff; the same move exists at Shopping list and Order of asks, whose tests become probes when the founder makes the offer or the refusal first; not a tell observed but a probe run, at the price of being wrong once, and it lies when the counterparty is not a partner but a committee that records the lapse as a fact.

Next-round hand: the investor's position is finally read after the wire, at the next round, in whether the fund takes its pro-rata, bridges a gap, or lets another lead mark the company down, which arrives too late for this raise and is the first tell for the next founder, because a fund's last three checks and its follow-ons are exactly the post-wire hands that other founders could not use in time, so the outside-readable ledger is made of other people's late tells; it lies when the fund's reserves ran out for reasons of vintage rather than belief, which Ledger's clock separates.

source.register: Operator-grade and concrete: partner hours, witness lists, filing dates, expiry clauses, no-shop lengths, anonymized customer lists, pro-rata; drawn from venture practice, medieval diplomatics, hostage negotiation, labor bargaining, auctions, and arms treaties.
source.mode: Analytical distinctions with composite observed cases; the thesis that every tell lies through its denominator is the author's analytical claim and is marked as such; Fuse length's reading of the founder's own price and Next-round hand's loop through other founders are speculative-analytical, kept with their modality visible.
source.via: practice-deep-ideonomy; two Fable fieldwork breaths; independent Fable editorial review
boundary_claim: Authored analytical fieldwork from composite cases in venture practice; no item is a documented history of any named fund, and the remote cases (charter witness lists, kidnappers' deadlines, treaty inspection clauses, wage reopeners, the prison yard's order of deference, the auction bidder's reserve question) are simplified to expose one mechanism each.

The seriation is an itinerary of where the founder must stand to see the carrier, not a ranking of reliability or importance; a tell late on the route is not a better tell, and map edges are conditional authored claims.

Every tell is read against a denominator, the fund's size, age, decision rule, and the partner's tenure, which the map treats as readable from the ledger; the public ledger is partial even where it exists, since uncalled capital is not public for most funds and announced checks undercount deployment, so Ledger's clock is an estimate from a sample and not a record; where the ledger is private, an unannounced vehicle or a family office, the readings above are undefined, and the map does not claim the ledger is always public.

Tells about the investor's future conduct, how they behave in a down round or whom they let the founder call, are outside the item type except at Next-round hand, where past conduct becomes the next founder's ledger; the map reads position, not character.

The map reads the investor and does not say what the founder should do with the reading; tells the investor can fake cheaply once the map is known, a second body sent as theater, a fuse set for show, are named as lies inside items but are not mapped as a class.

seriation.axis: Where the founder must stand for the carrier to be visible, and whether seeing it requires the founder to move: from the public record read before the first email (Ledger's clock), through the room, the following week, the diligence, and the paper, to a probe the founder must run (Let it lapse), and finally to the next round after the wire (Next-round hand), where the tell arrives too late for this raise.
seriation.note: An authored itinerary of residence, not a ranking of reliability; the tells readable from outside in a week are the first nine, the ledger, the room, the interval, the tense, and the holdable sentence, and the paper's tells are clocks and forecasts. Tense switch and Borrowed eyes sit after Queue interval because they are read at the second meeting, once the interval has been served and the investor's questions can be compared with the first meeting's; read at a first meeting they are the competitive check Borrowed eyes now excludes. The hinge adjacency is Back-channel spent → Fuse length: the last tell readable before paper and the first readable on it, and the adjacency teaches that a term sheet is a different object depending on whether the back-channel preceded it, a reservation that freezes the founder's alternatives or a decision that prices them. Let it lapse sits after the paper and before the wire because it is the only station where the founder is not a reader but an actor; Next-round hand closes the route because nothing later can be read for this raise, and its edge back to Ledger's clock says the route is a loop through other founders.

relations.label: If a fund's post-wire hands (pro-rata taken, gaps bridged, marks accepted) are what its founders could only read too late, and those hands reach the outside as announced participation or founder to founder, then the fund's outside-readable ledger is made of them, so the last tell of one raise is the first tell of the next; where a bridge or a mark stays private the loop closes only through founders who talk, never through the filings, and the loop closes through other founders and never through the same one.

relations.from: Ledger's clock: whether a yes is even available is read from the fund's own deployment record before the partner's appetite matters, since a fund in year four of a five-year investment period with half its capital uncalled must deploy and a fund that made nine investments in its first year and one in its third is holding reserves for its own portfolio, and both are visible in announced checks and filing dates before the first email; the carrier is the fund's ledger and not the partner, and it lies when the visible fund is not the vehicle that would write this check, an unannounced successor fund or an opportunity vehicle running on a different clock.
relations.to: Queue interval: an interval the founder is made to wait measures this deal's rank in a queue the founder cannot see, so the days before the second meeting read the partner's queue against whatever else that partner saw this week, and after signing the days before counsel returns a standard document read the fund's closing queue and whether it is waiting on something unsaid, a co-investor, a consent, a successor fund; it adds to lead-time-floors' Partner meeting, which reads what the calendar does to the founder's runway, by reading what the interval says about the investor's ordering, and it lies whenever the interval is the fund's clock rather than the partner's, in August, in December, or under must-deploy, which is why a fast second meeting from a fund late in its period reads the ledger and not the partner.
relations.label: If the ledger shows must-deploy, then a fast second meeting reads the fund's clock and not the partner's queue; the interval has no reading until the denominator has been read.

relations.from: Partner's name on the door: whether the person across the table can carry a deal is read from whose name sits on the fund's last deals, its board seats and its announcements, not from the title on the website, since a venture partner, a principal, or an operating partner can refer but cannot spend; it lies most instructively at the newly made partner whose name is on nothing because their first deal is still to come, and who therefore has the strongest motive in the building to close one, and it also lies at the partner hired laterally, whose deals sit on another fund's ledger, and at funds that seat a different partner on the board than the one who sponsored the deal, where the seat list reads bandwidth and not standing.
relations.to: Second body: partner attention is the fund's scarcest unit, so a second partner at the second meeting means the first has spent standing inside the partnership to bring one, as a medieval charter's witness list tells a historian which magnates the king needed present, while an associate-only follow-up, however warm, is still screening; a partner who writes the follow-up in their own words at midnight but cannot bring a second body is appetite without a vote, and the tell lies at a fund of two partners, where every meeting is a partner meeting and the reading must fall back to whether the meeting was moved to the founder's site.
relations.label: If the partner's name is on none of the fund's deals, then a warm second meeting without a second body is a referrer's enthusiasm and cannot become a yes; unless the partner is newly made, when the missing second body reads only that they have not yet learned to bring one.

relations.from: Back-channel spent: a call to a reference the founder offered is process, but a call to someone the founder did not offer, a former employee, a former investor, a rival's founder, costs the caller a favor and is spent only near the decision, so learning of it, usually from the person called, reads that the partner meeting is close and names the objection being tested; the reverse of lead-time-floors' Seeking is telling, since here the investor's search is visible to the founder, and the sharper reading is the call not made, because a term sheet issued with no back-channel is a reservation and not a decision wherever there was someone to call; it lies at large multi-stage funds whose research staff call everyone at screen, where the favor costs the partner nothing, and it is undefined at pre-seed, where no former employee, investor, or rival exists to be called and the absent call reads nothing.
relations.to: Fuse length: the expiry on a term sheet is priced against when the investor expects a rival sheet to arrive, so a short fuse reveals the investor's own estimate that the founder's alternatives are good, an outside estimate of the founder's price carried by the party who will pay it, as a kidnapper's deadline reveals what the kidnapper believes the family can raise by then; it also reads the fund's clock when the close-by date is the fund's own, and it lies at funds that put a fuse on every sheet as house style, which founders who took their paper can tell you and which only Let it lapse can test.
relations.label: If a sheet arrives before any back-channel was spent, then its fuse sits on a reservation and the founder's alternatives are being frozen rather than outbid; if after, the fuse sits on a decision and reads the investor's estimate of the founder's price; the same clause is two objects.

relations.from: Neighbor in the portfolio: if the fund already holds a company in the founder's market, the meeting's purpose is set before it starts, and the tell is whether the partner names the neighbor unprompted, since an undisclosed neighbor makes the meeting intelligence gathered for it; it adds to cooperative-masks' alliance proposed to inventory your capabilities the check that can be run from the portfolio page before the alliance is proposed, and it lies at a fund that runs an index strategy and will honestly own two rivals, which its ledger shows as other such pairs.
relations.to: Shopping list: diligence questions divide by whether the answer is useful to someone other than the decider, so named customers with prices, a pipeline by account, and a roadmap by quarter are transferable to a portfolio company while the reason a cohort churned is not, and the test is whether the investor accepts anonymized accounts and founder-chosen reference names, since a decider needs the shape and a shopper needs the names; it lies at late-stage funds whose cohort work needs account-level data, separated by their willingness to route it through a third-party quality-of-earnings firm that returns only the shape.
relations.label: If the fund holds a neighbor, then a request that fails the anonymization test is read as the neighbor's list rather than as late-stage cohort work, and the growth-fund excuse is unavailable to it.

relations.from: Borrowed eyes: an investor who asks who else is in before any question about the company, and whose questions about the company arrive only after the answer names a lead, or never, holds a position that is a function of another investor's, so the founder is reading the wrong node and every later tell from this investor should be re-read as a tell about the lead it follows, a day late; not the same question asked first by an investor who then inspects, which checks whether the round is already spoken for, and it lies when the question is about round mechanics from a fund that never leads and honestly needs a lead to set terms, which its ledger shows as a record of follows.
relations.to: Tense switch: an investor still deciding asks about the past, why the cohort churned, why this architecture, while an investor who has decided asks about the deal, round size, who else is in, whether there is room to lead, and the switch usually precedes any spoken yes by days; the sharpest form is the allocation question, how much can we take, which is addressed to the other investors through the founder, as an auction bidder who asks about the reserve has stopped inspecting the lot; it lies when a partner asks round size first to check the fund's check-size fit, which is a size question and not an allocation question.
relations.label: If the first question was who else is in and inspection never followed the answer, then this investor's tense switch is an echo of the lead's, a day later, and reads only that the lead has switched; the founder reads the lead's questions and discards this investor's.

relations.from: Let it lapse: some tells exist only if the founder moves, so an expiry allowed to pass by a day reads whether the fuse was real, since a re-issued sheet shows the investor feared losing the deal more than being seen to bluff and a withdrawn one shows the clock was the fund's, as a deadline a kidnapper lets pass unacted reveals the deadline was a bluff; the same move exists at Shopping list and Order of asks, whose tests become probes when the founder makes the offer or the refusal first; not a tell observed but a probe run, at the price of being wrong once, and it lies when the counterparty is not a partner but a committee that records the lapse as a fact.
relations.to: Fuse length: the expiry on a term sheet is priced against when the investor expects a rival sheet to arrive, so a short fuse reveals the investor's own estimate that the founder's alternatives are good, an outside estimate of the founder's price carried by the party who will pay it, as a kidnapper's deadline reveals what the kidnapper believes the family can raise by then; it also reads the fund's clock when the close-by date is the fund's own, and it lies at funds that put a fuse on every sheet as house style, which founders who took their paper can tell you and which only Let it lapse can test.
relations.label: Can test: if the founder lets the fuse pass by a day, a re-issued sheet shows the fuse was priced on the founder's alternatives and a withdrawn one shows the clock was the fund's; the fuse has no settled reading until the founder moves.

exploration.first_question: What does an investor do, rather than say, that reveals where their decision actually sits, and which of those doings can a founder read from outside in a week and which only after a term sheet?
exploration.changed_question: What must the founder know about the investor's cost of each carrier before any behavior becomes a reading at all? Sharpening each item's lie case in breath one produced the same shape every time: the tell lies where the carrier is cheap or dear for that investor for reasons unrelated to this deal, a two-partner fund where a second body costs nothing, a fund late in its period where speed is the ledger's, a house template where the fuse is nobody's. So the question became one about denominators, and it turned up tells whose reading transfers to another node (Borrowed eyes), tells that exist only if the founder moves (Let it lapse), and the tell that arrives too late and becomes the next founder's ledger (Next-round hand), which closed the route into a loop the first framing had drawn as a line.
exploration.new_member: Let it lapse: some tells exist only if the founder moves, so an expiry allowed to pass by a day reads whether the fuse was real, since a re-issued sheet shows the investor feared losing the deal more than being seen to bluff and a withdrawn one shows the clock was the fund's, as a deadline a kidnapper lets pass unacted reveals the deadline was a bluff; the same move exists at Shopping list and Order of asks, whose tests become probes when the founder makes the offer or the refusal first; not a tell observed but a probe run, at the price of being wrong once, and it lies when the counterparty is not a partner but a committee that records the lapse as a fact.

priorities.item: Holdable sentence: an investor's words are read by whether they could later be quoted back against the speaker, so we would love to see more traction is a pass that keeps a free option on the company, while at this revenue with this retention, call me and we move in a week binds a metric, a threshold, and a date, as an employer who names a wage reopener date has conceded something and one who says we will look at it next year has not; the carrier is the cost of being quoted, and it lies when a fund rule such as a stage floor makes the vagueness honest rather than option-keeping, which is checked against the ledger.
priorities.why: It is the cheapest tell on the route, read from the wording of passes the founder already holds, and if quotability predicts later conversion it turns every pass into a sorted follow-up list rather than a pile.
priorities.next_question: Take the passes received in one raise and sort each by whether it names a metric, a threshold, and a date; at the next raise, re-approach both sorted sets with the same update and record which set converts to a meeting within a week, to learn whether the holdable pass predicts a later yes or is merely a politer no.

priorities.item: Next-round hand: the investor's position is finally read after the wire, at the next round, in whether the fund takes its pro-rata, bridges a gap, or lets another lead mark the company down, which arrives too late for this raise and is the first tell for the next founder, because a fund's last three checks and its follow-ons are exactly the post-wire hands that other founders could not use in time, so the outside-readable ledger is made of other people's late tells; it lies when the fund's reserves ran out for reasons of vintage rather than belief, which Ledger's clock separates.
priorities.why: Low plausibility that any week-one tell predicts the post-wire hand, high generative promise: if one does, the loop back to Ledger's clock becomes a way to read a fund's future conduct from other founders' first meetings, and if none does, the map's outside-readable half is honestly severed from what it most wants to know.
priorities.next_question: For one fund, list its portfolio's next rounds over three years and mark where it took pro-rata, bridged, or let another lead mark the company down; then ask those founders what the partner did in the first two weeks (second body, tense switch, back-channel) and see whether any week-one tell sorts the hands better than the fund's vintage does.

gate.standard: declared type, close-neighbor discriminator, boundary case, and form inference
gate.independent_review: Fable critic: admitted after repairing six items (a false 'exactly one case', a neighbor collapse between Borrowed eyes and Tense switch on the competitive-check case, three missing lie cases at pre-seed, rule-based passes, and carried-forward terms, and one clause of Let it lapse that restated its neighbors) and two edge labels, and after noting that the declared type's 'rather than says' undersells its own members, which are read off the unpriced cost inside a calendar, a signature, or a sentence; the boundary claim now concedes partial public ledgers and lists the prison-yard and auction-reserve cases among the simplified remote cases.

neighbors.left: Fuse length: the expiry on a term sheet is priced against when the investor expects a rival sheet to arrive, so a short fuse reveals the investor's own estimate that the founder's alternatives are good, an outside estimate of the founder's price carried by the party who will pay it, as a kidnapper's deadline reveals what the kidnapper believes the family can raise by then; it also reads the fund's clock when the close-by date is the fund's own, and it lies at funds that put a fuse on every sheet as house style, which founders who took their paper can tell you and which only Let it lapse can test.
neighbors.right: Exclusivity as confession: the length of the no-shop the investor asks for measures the work the investor has not yet done and the room to walk it wants to keep, so sixty days from a fund that has spent no back-channel is an option and ten days from one that has is a close; it adds to lead-time-floors' No-shop, which reads what the lock does to the founder's clock, by reading what the lock's length says about the investor's remaining doubt, and it lies where the length was set by counsel's template rather than by the partner.
neighbors.separating_case: A sheet with a forty-eight-hour fuse and a sixty-day no-shop: the fuse says the investor fears a rival sheet this week, the no-shop says the investor has not decided, and together they read an investor trying to freeze the market before doing the work; a sheet with a ten-day fuse and a ten-day no-shop is the opposite object, an investor who has decided and fears nobody. The two clocks read two different states, the investor's estimate of the founder's alternatives and the investor's own remaining doubt, and can point in opposite directions on one page.

checks.boundary_case: Which founders the investor lets you call is a tempting nonmember: it is read from what the investor does rather than says, but it reads how the investor will behave after the wire, their conduct in a down round, not where their decision on this deal sits, so it is out of type. Next-round hand is in on exactly that contrast, since it reads the fund's position (reserves, belief) at the point where past conduct becomes another founder's ledger.
checks.form_inference: The map shows a loop the sequence conceals: Next-round hand → Ledger's clock, where the last tell of one raise, unusable in time, is the first tell of the next founder's, so the outside-readable half of the route is made of other founders' late tells. It shows a dependency, Ledger's clock → Queue interval and Partner's name on the door → Second body, where a behavior has no reading until its denominator has been read. It shows a fork, Back-channel spent → Fuse length, where the same expiry clause is a reservation or a decision depending on what preceded it. It shows a passage between nodes, Borrowed eyes → Tense switch, where the reading transfers to a different investor and this one's switch is kept only as an echo that says the lead has switched. And it shows a passage between levels, Let it lapse → Fuse length, from observation to experiment, where a tell has no settled reading until the founder acts.
checks.target_preserved: Judged by the Fable critic in a fresh context: the item type is real and sharper than declared (a cost whose reading the investor did not price in, whether it sits in a calendar, a signature, or a sentence), the Fuse/Exclusivity pair separates as authored, the loop and the fork are real; six items were repaired for false precision, a neighbor collapse between Borrowed eyes and Tense switch on the competitive-check case, three missing lie cases, and one restating clause, and the strange members (a tell that reads the founder's own price off the investor's fear, a tell that transfers to another node, a tell that exists only if the founder moves, a tell that arrives too late and becomes someone else's first tell) are kept as mechanisms rather than softened into a list of red flags.

name: dilution-carriers
of: A carrier, whether a clause, a form, a clock, a document, or a decision, through which ownership or control drains from a party by a route other than the round price, named with the moment it is agreed, who typically understood it at signing, the arithmetic in one illustrative case, and what its amount waits on, since the drain may be computable on the cap table at signing, on a clock, at the next round's price, at a person's leaving, at the exit, or never as a number at all because what drains is control.
items: Pool before the price: the lead requires the unallocated option pool to be enlarged before the round and counted inside the pre-money, so the pool's dilution falls entirely on the holders who were there before the money while the headline pre-money is untouched; agreed in one term-sheet line, 'pre-money includes a fifteen percent post-closing pool', understood by the lead always and by the founder when counsel explains it; with an eight million pre and two million in, a fifteen-percent post pool is one and a half million carved from the eight, so the founders' shares are priced at six and a half; not the pool itself, which real hires will need, but which side of the price line it sits on, and the tell is a pool sized to a round number rather than to a hiring plan.

Additive slices: under the post-money SAFE each check buys a percentage fixed as of the moment before the priced round and immune to every later SAFE, so the slices add and the founders alone pay for each one; agreed one check at a time with investors who never see the others, understood by the form's author, who published the arithmetic, and not by the founder who reads 'post-money' as a valuation word; five hundred thousand at a five million cap, a million at ten, a million and a half at fifteen is ten, ten, and ten percent, thirty percent gone before the Series A prices a share; not stacking as such, which pre-money notes also do while diluting one another, but immunity, which makes each slice a fixed charge on the common.

Below the threshold: grants each too small to be argued over, an advisor's quarter point, a consultant's half, a friend's tenth, are approved without the process a large grant gets and sum above the threshold the process exists for; agreed over coffee, understood by nobody as a total; six advisors at a half point each, vesting monthly with no cliff, is three percent, a seed check's slice with no check behind it; not the size of any grant but the granularity that keeps each one below attention, and the tell is that nobody in the room can name the sum.

Warrant on the loan: venture debt carries warrant coverage, a fraction of the principal in warrants struck at the last round's price, so a lender who bore credit risk and no equity risk holds equity if the company rises; agreed in the loan agreement and carried in the debt file rather than the round documents, so it is priced at zero in every conversation that is not about the exit and missing from the cap table the founder quotes from memory; three million borrowed with ten-percent coverage at a ten-million post is three hundred thousand of shares at last-round price, three percent of the company on a loan that also charges twelve; not interest, which is paid in cash and ends, but a share count fixed at signing whose value waits on the exit, and the tell is a cap table that omits the debt file.

Interest that converts: a convertible note accrues interest that is never paid in cash but converts with the principal at the cap, so the dilution is a function of how long the note waits for a price; agreed as a rate everyone reads as an accounting line; two million at eight percent open for thirty months adds four hundred thousand that converts at a ten million cap into a slice of roughly four percent nobody wrote a check for; not the discount, which is fixed at signing, but a clock, and a delayed round pays for the delay in shares.

Dividend nobody pays: preferred stock carries a cumulative dividend, accruing at a stated rate and payable only at liquidation, so the preference stack grows on a clock while every financial statement shows no dividend paid; agreed as a line the founder reads as a formality because the company will never declare one, understood by the investor as a return that compounds whether or not the company does; fifty million of preferred at eight percent cumulative over five years adds twenty million to the preference before a dollar reaches common, and the sum is on no cap table; not interest that converts, which becomes shares at the next price, but a claim that stays ahead of shares until the end.

Cap as option: a valuation cap is a ceiling, not a price, so the SAFE converts at the lower of the cap and the discounted round price, and the holder is long an option whose value grows with the uncertainty of the next round; agreed when the founder treats the cap as the valuation she raised at, understood by the investor as a floor on his percentage; a SAFE at a ten million cap converts at ten if the A prices at twenty and at six if the A prices at six, so the 'ten million round' was a ten-or-less round; not a discount, which is a fixed ratio, but a payoff bent at the cap, and the tell is a founder quoting the cap as her last valuation.

Ratchet after the fact: anti-dilution resets an earlier round's conversion price when a later round prices lower, so the earlier investor receives shares as if she had bought at the lower price and the common pays for them; agreed in a clause the founder skips because she does not intend a down round, understood by the investor as the term that makes a high price safe; under a full ratchet a Series A that bought a quarter at four dollars sees a B at two and doubles its share count before the B buys a share, and broad-based weighted average softens this by the B's size; observed in Square's 2015 offering, where a Series E floor of $18.56 against a nine-dollar offer issued the E about ten million extra shares, as reported; not a repricing, which the investor did not buy, but a repricing in one direction only, so the earlier money holds a put on the later price.

Reset with the trigger in the other hand: the Series A puts a founder's already-vested shares back on a schedule with a repurchase right at cost, so a founder three years in and three-quarters vested is a quarter vested again; agreed under the sentence 'we need you committed' and understood by both sides as a commitment device, but the board that can end her employment is, after the round, a board the investor sits on, and forfeited shares are retired, which lifts every remaining holder pro rata including the one who voted; a founder with thirty percent removed twelve months after the reset keeps under half of her shares, and the seventeen percent of the company that returns is spread over whoever remains; not vesting, which any hire accepts, but a forfeiture whose trigger sits with a board on which its beneficiaries vote.

Ninety-day guillotine: vested options must be exercised within ninety days of leaving, paying the strike and the tax on the spread, or they lapse back to the pool, so the carrier of an employee's ownership back to the company is a purchase price on the exit door, due on the day she can least afford it; agreed in the plan document every hire signs unread, written by counsel under a tax rule; fifty thousand vested options at a two-dollar strike against a twenty-dollar appraisal is a hundred thousand in cash and a nine-hundred-thousand spread the tax bill can treat as income, so a departing engineer with a mortgage forfeits ownership she spent four years earning; not a vesting term, since the shares had vested, but a toll on keeping them, and what lapses returns to a pool the same board regrants, so the beneficiary is whoever is hired next and the founder whose next refill is smaller.

Stack that eats the common: each round's preferred takes its money back before common sees anything, so the founder's percentage is a share of the exit only above the price at which conversion beats preference, and below it a good price pays the common almost nothing; agreed round by round as 'one times non-participating, standard', understood by every investor as the whole point and read by the founder as a percentage; fifty million raised at one times, exit at sixty, the preferred take fifty and a founder with twenty percent takes two million from a sale the press reports at sixty million; not the round price, which set her percentage truly, but a floor under each round that becomes the entire payout when the exit lands near the raise, and the tell is the conversion price, above which the cap table becomes honest again.

Dip twice: participating preferred takes its preference and then its pro-rata share of what is left, so there is no exit price at which the cap table's percentage becomes the holder's share of proceeds until the participation cap is reached; agreed as one word after 'preferred', understood by the investor as the term that makes the cap table lie at every price; ten million for a quarter, exit at forty, takes ten plus a quarter of thirty, seventeen and a half, forty-four percent of the exit for twenty-five percent of the company; not the stack, which vanishes at the conversion point, but a stack with no such point below the cap, so the arithmetic must be run at every exit price rather than once.

Secondary that grows the stack: a buyer of founder or early-holder common in a secondary demands the shares be reclassified into the latest preferred, so a preference is created on shares that carried none, the stack grows by the secondary's size, and no cash reaches the company; agreed between seller and buyer with a board consent the company gives to make the sale happen, understood by the buyer's counsel, and invisible to the employees, since nothing was issued; a founder who sells five million of common at the Series C price adds five million to the stack ahead of the shares she kept and ahead of everyone's options; not the sale itself, which moves ownership at a price, but the reclassification, which moves a claim.

Carve-out at the door: when the exit price sits inside or barely above the stack, the preferred agree a management carve-out, a share of proceeds paid to named, still-employed executives before the waterfall, so the same founder is paid as a manager and nothing as a shareholder, and every common holder who left gets nothing; agreed at the exit, by the board, understood by the board and by no one who has already gone; a hundred-and-fifteen-million sale against a hundred and ten of preference would pay the common five million, and a ten-percent carve-out taken off the top pays eleven and a half million to the four managers named and zero to two hundred option holders and the departed co-founder, so the carve-out drains the common only in the band from the top of the stack up to that top divided by one minus the carve-out fraction, a hundred and twenty-two here, while inside the stack the same carve-out is paid from the preferred's own money and drains the common nothing; not the stack, which is the cause, but the exception bought from it, and it forks the founder from the people who built the thing with her.

Headline bought with terms: the investor grants the valuation the founder needs for the press, the hires, and the next round, and takes it back in the waterfall, so the price is real in one ledger and false in the other; agreed with both parties knowing and each believing the other's ledger is the one that will not matter; twenty million for twenty percent at a hundred post with one-times participating pays the investor forty-six million on a hundred-and-fifty exit, while twenty million for twenty-nine percent at seventy post with one-times non-participating pays forty-three, so the higher valuation was the dearer one; adds to what-a-price-does' price for the stranger's eyes the compensating term that makes the stranger's number cheap for the party who granted it; not a bad price but a price paid in a currency the price does not show.

Ten votes a share: the founder's class carries ten votes, so control is conserved while economics drain, and the leak is in the sunset and the transfer clauses, since the class converts to common on sale, on death, on leaving, or on a date; agreed at incorporation or at the offering, understood by the founder as permanent and by counsel as a schedule; eleven percent of the economics with fifty-five percent of the vote, until a divorce transfers a two-point block that converts on transfer and the vote falls under half; not control as such but control on a clock the founder does not see as a clock, and the tell is that the class's conversion events are listed on a page she never turned to.

Veto without votes: protective provisions give the preferred a class vote over a sale, a new round, debt, the budget, and the pool, so a twenty-percent holder can block anything while the cap table shows nothing, since the control lives in the charter and not in the count; agreed as 'standard protective provisions', understood by the investor as the deal and by the founder as boilerplate; the reverse of ten votes a share, economics intact and control gone, and a board seat granted to a two-percent seed holder is the same carrier held by a body instead of a class; not a majority but a list of things a majority may not do, and no arithmetic ever shows it.

source.register: Operator-grade and concrete: term-sheet clauses, plan documents, loan agreements, charters, and cap-table arithmetic in round numbers; drawn from venture financing, venture debt, employee equity plans, secondaries, acquisitions, and dual-class charters.
source.mode: Analytical distinctions over standard-form instruments with illustrative round-number arithmetic; the 'who understood it at signing' clauses are the author's generalization about a typical asymmetry and not findings; one case, Square's 2015 offering, is documented as reported, and every other case is constructed.
source.via: practice-deep-ideonomy; two Fable fieldwork breaths; independent Fable editorial review
boundary_claim: Authored analytical fieldwork over standard-form instruments (venture term sheets, the post-money SAFE, venture loan warrants, option plans, protective provisions, dual-class charters), each simplified to one mechanism; not a legal or tax guide, and jurisdiction, plan design, and negotiation change several of them.
The arithmetic is illustrative in round numbers and belongs to no company; the single documented case, Square's 2015 ratchet, is cited as reported and not analyzed from filings.

The claims about who understood a term at signing describe a typical asymmetry the author asserts, not a finding; a founder with counsel who reads the documents can understand every carrier here, and the map does not claim otherwise.

The itinerary sorts by what the carrier's amount waits on, not by the size or frequency of the drain; no claim of exhaustiveness, and carriers where the headline price is itself the route (a recap, a cram-down, a low seed price) are out by the item type.

Adjacent admitted items and what ours add: Headline bought with terms adds to what-a-price-does' Price for the stranger's eyes the compensating term; Ratchet after the fact runs the opposite way from clean-exits' Fade by formula, since the price rather than the holder pulls it and the preferred gains; Ninety-day guillotine is the exit-door toll on the asset runway-illusions' Reach the cliff describes arriving; Veto without votes is live legal power, not ghost-leverages' habit.

seriation.axis: What the carrier's amount waits on before it can be computed: from nothing, since a cap table at signing computes it to the last share (Pool before the price), through a clock, then the next round's price, then a person's leaving, then the exit price and the room at the exit (with Headline bought with terms held back past the room as the hinge), to nothing again for the opposite reason, because what drains is control and no share count ever shows it (Veto without votes).
seriation.note: An authored itinerary, not a ranking of size, harm, or frequency. Pool before the price opens it because a spreadsheet at signing settles the whole drain; Veto without votes closes it because no spreadsheet at any time shows it. The consequential adjacency is Cap as option → Ratchet after the fact: a SAFE cap is anti-dilution for money not yet converted, and anti-dilution is a cap for money already in, so the same put on the next price is written twice on the itinerary, once before the money converts and once after, and a founder who negotiates the cap hard and skips the anti-dilution clause has defended one side of the same term. Warrant on the loan sits at the boundary between the signing stage and the clock stage on purpose: its share count is fixed at signing and its value waits on the exit, and it is hidden not by arithmetic but by the document it lives in. Headline bought with terms waits on the exit price and by the axis belongs beside Stack that eats the common and Dip twice; it is placed after Carve-out at the door as an authored inversion, because it is the hinge. That hinge is Headline bought with terms → Ten votes a share: the valuation and the vote are the two things a founder keeps visibly, and they are the two the investors grant most easily, because the waterfall and the veto list are where the deal is; past the hinge the drain has no arithmetic. Read the whole walk under one conservation law: percentages sum to a hundred, so every immunity granted to one holder is a charge on whoever lacks it, and the founders and the option holders are the parties who never hold one.

relations.from: Pool before the price: the lead requires the unallocated option pool to be enlarged before the round and counted inside the pre-money, so the pool's dilution falls entirely on the holders who were there before the money while the headline pre-money is untouched; agreed in one term-sheet line, 'pre-money includes a fifteen percent post-closing pool', understood by the lead always and by the founder when counsel explains it; with an eight million pre and two million in, a fifteen-percent post pool is one and a half million carved from the eight, so the founders' shares are priced at six and a half; not the pool itself, which real hires will need, but which side of the price line it sits on, and the tell is a pool sized to a round number rather than to a hiring plan.
relations.to: Below the threshold: grants each too small to be argued over, an advisor's quarter point, a consultant's half, a friend's tenth, are approved without the process a large grant gets and sum above the threshold the process exists for; agreed over coffee, understood by nobody as a total; six advisors at a half point each, vesting monthly with no cliff, is three percent, a seed check's slice with no check behind it; not the size of any grant but the granularity that keeps each one below attention, and the tell is that nobody in the room can name the sum.
relations.label: If the pool is sized inside the pre-money, then the grants below the threshold are drawn from shares the pre-money holders paid for, and the next lead sizes the refill inside the next pre-money, so at every round the holders who were there before the money buy the pool that the small grants emptied; the loop closes at every term sheet that says 'pre-money includes the pool'.

relations.from: Interest that converts: a convertible note accrues interest that is never paid in cash but converts with the principal at the cap, so the dilution is a function of how long the note waits for a price; agreed as a rate everyone reads as an accounting line; two million at eight percent open for thirty months adds four hundred thousand that converts at a ten million cap into a slice of roughly four percent nobody wrote a check for; not the discount, which is fixed at signing, but a clock, and a delayed round pays for the delay in shares.
relations.to: Dividend nobody pays: preferred stock carries a cumulative dividend, accruing at a stated rate and payable only at liquidation, so the preference stack grows on a clock while every financial statement shows no dividend paid; agreed as a line the founder reads as a formality because the company will never declare one, understood by the investor as a return that compounds whether or not the company does; fifty million of preferred at eight percent cumulative over five years adds twenty million to the preference before a dollar reaches common, and the sum is on no cap table; not interest that converts, which becomes shares at the next price, but a claim that stays ahead of shares until the end.
relations.label: If the note converts into a preferred series that carries a cumulative dividend, then the clock that ran on the note restarts one level up on a larger principal, and what accrued as shares at the next price now accrues as preference at the exit.

relations.from: Cap as option: a valuation cap is a ceiling, not a price, so the SAFE converts at the lower of the cap and the discounted round price, and the holder is long an option whose value grows with the uncertainty of the next round; agreed when the founder treats the cap as the valuation she raised at, understood by the investor as a floor on his percentage; a SAFE at a ten million cap converts at ten if the A prices at twenty and at six if the A prices at six, so the 'ten million round' was a ten-or-less round; not a discount, which is a fixed ratio, but a payoff bent at the cap, and the tell is a founder quoting the cap as her last valuation.
relations.to: Ratchet after the fact: anti-dilution resets an earlier round's conversion price when a later round prices lower, so the earlier investor receives shares as if she had bought at the lower price and the common pays for them; agreed in a clause the founder skips because she does not intend a down round, understood by the investor as the term that makes a high price safe; under a full ratchet a Series A that bought a quarter at four dollars sees a B at two and doubles its share count before the B buys a share, and broad-based weighted average softens this by the B's size; observed in Square's 2015 offering, where a Series E floor of $18.56 against a nine-dollar offer issued the E about ten million extra shares, as reported; not a repricing, which the investor did not buy, but a repricing in one direction only, so the earlier money holds a put on the later price.
relations.label: If the A prices below the cap, the SAFE takes the round price and the cap was a ratchet before the fact; if it prices above, the SAFE converts at the cap into preferred whose anti-dilution is the same put written on the B; either way the holder is never without a put on the next price.

relations.from: Ratchet after the fact: anti-dilution resets an earlier round's conversion price when a later round prices lower, so the earlier investor receives shares as if she had bought at the lower price and the common pays for them; agreed in a clause the founder skips because she does not intend a down round, understood by the investor as the term that makes a high price safe; under a full ratchet a Series A that bought a quarter at four dollars sees a B at two and doubles its share count before the B buys a share, and broad-based weighted average softens this by the B's size; observed in Square's 2015 offering, where a Series E floor of $18.56 against a nine-dollar offer issued the E about ten million extra shares, as reported; not a repricing, which the investor did not buy, but a repricing in one direction only, so the earlier money holds a put on the later price.
relations.to: Pool before the price: the lead requires the unallocated option pool to be enlarged before the round and counted inside the pre-money, so the pool's dilution falls entirely on the holders who were there before the money while the headline pre-money is untouched; agreed in one term-sheet line, 'pre-money includes a fifteen percent post-closing pool', understood by the lead always and by the founder when counsel explains it; with an eight million pre and two million in, a fifteen-percent post pool is one and a half million carved from the eight, so the founders' shares are priced at six and a half; not the pool itself, which real hires will need, but which side of the price line it sits on, and the tell is a pool sized to a round number rather than to a hiring plan.
relations.label: If a down round triggers the ratchet, then the employee options are underwater and the new lead requires a refreshed pool inside the new pre-money, so the common is diluted by the ratchet and again by the refresh while the ratcheted preferred is diluted by neither.
